rst31-cooking1-beef-table.title: Link beef cuts to characteristics and dishes
rst31-cooking1-beef-table.text: Beef shoulder is slightly firm lean meat rich in extractives and collagen, used for soups and stews. Brisket has layered lean/fat and is firm, with stewing examples. Chuck roll has somewhat more connective tissue, moderate fat and flavour, used for shabu-shabu, sukiyaki and grilling. Compare fine-textured rib loin in similar thin-sliced dishes or steaks with sirloin in steaks/roast beef. Tenderloin is fine, tender and lean for beef cutlets or steaks. Rump is flavourful tender lean meat for steaks or roast beef. Short plate has layered fat, coarse texture, marbling potential and rich flavour, used for stew or grilled short-rib dishes. Inside round is described as the leanest listed beef cut and has steak, roast, grilling and stewing examples. Outside round is lean, coarse and firm, suited to thin/small stir-fry pieces or stewing. Shank is firm and sinewy but long cooking releases collagen for stew or curry. These are quality-selection descriptions, separate from safe heating conditions.

rst31-cooking1-pork-table.title: Choose pork cuts appropriately
rst31-cooking1-pork-table.text: Pork shoulder is coarse and fairly firm with some fat, lending flavour to cubed stews and pork-and-beans. Collar/chuck roll is coarse, firm and rich; cut connective tissue before curry, roast pork or ginger pork. Loin has fine texture and moderate fat, with outer-fat flavour used in tonkatsu, pork shabu-shabu and loin ham. Tenderloin is fine, tender and lean yet rich in vitamin B 1, used for cutlets or sautéing. Outside leg is mild lean meat; leg is lean and fine-textured for sautéing, grilling and boneless ham. The source ranks leg’s B 1 after tenderloin. Belly has alternating lean/fat for curry, dongpo pork and braises. Bone-in belly is called spare ribs. Orders should identify animal, cut and bone status, not dish name alone.

rst31-cooking1-chicken-table.title: Compare chicken texture and uses
rst31-cooking1-chicken-table.text: Thigh has richness from intramuscular fat and firm tissue and is described as slightly firmer than breast; link it to teriyaki, chicken cutlets and karaage. Breast is tender, mild and lean, with simmered/steamed chicken examples. Tenderloin is the leanest listed chicken example, mild and used for fritters or steamed egg custard. Wings are collagen-rich for frying, braising or yakitori. For example, repeat back “breast” when asked for steamed chicken rather than assuming every cut has the same texture. Cut comparisons concern quality, not proof of safe heating.

rst31-cooking1-fish-season-spring.title: Spring seafood examples
rst31-cooking1-fish-season-spring.text: The source lists sawara, asari clams, wakame, funa carp and red sea bream as spring seasonal examples. Seasonality varies with region and climate, so distinguish the table from today’s species, origin and delivery condition. For example, match names and seasons in the preparation sheet, then check actual delivery labels. “In season” alone does not authorise raw consumption.

Similar colour does not mean the same group or ingredient name. For example, record both group and item when sorting deliveries and compare the goods with labels. This classification does not establish allergen status or raw-food safety.

rst31-cooking1-preparation-separation.title: Preparation washing, disinfection and task changes
rst31-cooking1-preparation-separation.text: Calculate requirements and remove only what is needed, washing off soil, dirt and foreign material. Apply specified disinfection when the ingredient/process requires it; washing and disinfection are not identical. Removing inedible parts, peeling, suitable cutting and marinating also count as preparation. Work promptly once ingredients are out, and thaw appropriately, such as in refrigeration or under running water. If benches, knives and boards cannot be separated by use, wash/disinfect thoroughly after use before switching. Do not prepare raw ingredients and plate finished food in the same place/time or have one person prepare, cook and plate simultaneously. When a raw-preparation worker switches to plating, finish that task and confirm clean surfaces, equipment and hands before restarting.

rst31-cooking1-cut-source-dimensions.title: Distinguish the source’s cutting dimensions
rst31-cooking1-cut-source-dimensions.text: The source example gives shikishi as roughly 3 cm squares and dice as 1 cm cubes. Hyoshigi is shown as 4–5 cm-long sticks with a 1 cm square section; its tanzaku entry states 4–5 cm length and 1 cm thickness. Compare flat tanzaku with stick-shaped hyoshigi, but do not apply these numbers to every recipe. Check the cut’s name separately from store-sample thickness/length when preparing ingredients for one dish. Ask the responsible person rather than independently changing conflicting dimensions or names.

rst31-cooking1-cooking-quality-examples.title: Read rice-cooking and boiling-water examples
rst31-cooking1-cooking-quality-examples.text: Heat rice after water absorption; more water relative to rice gives a softer result and less gives a firmer one. The source uses at least 98℃ for at least 20 minutes to explain rice-starch gelatinisation. This concerns cooking quality, not a universal food-safety standard or setting for every cooker. Its boiling-water examples associate salt with limiting shape breakdown, vinegar with brightening white ingredients, and baking soda with brightening green vegetables. Boiled edamame and potatoes are example dishes. Even when checking the purpose for green vegetables, follow the recipe/store directions rather than adding the same amount to all foods.

rst31-cooking1-frying-example.title: Frying-temperature examples and oil-quality checks
rst31-cooking1-frying-example.text: Frying places ingredients in heated oil. The source’s roughly 180℃ is an oil-temperature example, not a food-centre pass value or universal setting for every dish. Examples include croquettes, tempura, breaded fried foods and karaage. Check oil quality each use and notice changes such as conspicuous foaming during heating. A correct display does not replace checking oil condition, batch size and heating through the centre. Report abnormalities and decide replacement under store criteria.

rst31-cooking1-simmer-quality.title: Simmering-liquid examples and texture control
rst31-cooking1-simmer-quality.text: Simmering heats ingredients in liquid seasoned with sugar, soy sauce and similar ingredients; examples include meat-and-potato stew, mixed simmered dishes, kinpira and braised pork belly. The source describes normally boiling seasoned liquid as 100℃ and also gives long cooking around 70–80℃ as a quality example to avoid tightening tissues strongly. This does not authorise skipping safety checks at lower temperatures. Aims include tenderness, gentle setting, easier fish-bone separation and reduced odour. Distinguish liquid conditions from food-centre heating checks and follow store procedures.

rst31-cooking1-nonheat-mixing.title: Unheated finishing and changes in dressed dishes
rst31-cooking1-nonheat-mixing.text: Unheated preparation uses no flame or heat to make ingredients ready to eat after necessary washing, disinfection and preparation. Dressing/mixing combines treated ingredients with seasonings, as in vegetable salad, steamed-and-mashed potato salad or marinades. Ingredients may have been heated without reheating after mixing. Vinegar is used to explain bacterial-growth inhibition, but water released by food dilutes it and changes both taste and inhibitory conditions. If a prepared dish becomes watery, do not declare it safe merely by adding vinegar; check preparation time, storage and planned service.

rst31-cooking1-machine-feature-groups.title: Check heat sources, capacity and cooling roles
rst31-cooking1-machine-feature-groups.text: Gas ranges and Chinese gas ranges use gas; IH ranges use electricity. Steamers use steam, fryers oil and noodle boilers hot water; griddles serve grilling/sautéing. Cabinet rice cookers cook bulk rice, tabletop cookers cook on the counter, and rice warmers hold cooked rice hot. Compare bulk grilling/sautéing/simmering in braising pans, bulk sautéing/simmering in tilting kettles and conveyor heating in jet ovens. Distinguish storage, display and worktop refrigeration, walk-in rooms, ice makers and rapid cooked-food cooling equipment. The source calls vacuum coolers more powerful than blast chillers, but this does not rank every model. Check nameplates/manuals for suitability to actual food, capacity and target process.

rst31-cooking1-safety-habits-clothing.title: Connect familiarity, haste and clothing to safety checks
rst31-cooking1-safety-habits-clothing.text: Safety cannot rely on one attentive person. Everyone follows agreed work without skipping steps because of haste or inconvenience or assuming “it should be fine.” Keep checks even in daily tasks. Lifting an unchecked heavy pot, cutting while looking elsewhere and leaving a heat source unattended cause different accidents. Uniforms also protect: some chef coats are described as harder to ignite, not every garment as certified flame-retardant. Wear the specified well-fitting uniform correctly rather than substituting freely, and do not tread down shoe heels, which increases fall risk.

rst31-cooking1-load-source-numbers.title: Do not treat load/fill guides as safety guarantees
rst31-cooking1-load-source-numbers.text: The source gives manual-load examples of 35–40% of body weight and liquid filling around eight-tenths of a pot. These are not safe limits for everyone. Ministry back-pain prevention guidance considers frequency, posture, build and health as well as weight and prioritises reducing manual load with equipment/trolleys. Do not decide solo carrying from body weight alone; discuss dividing loads, aids or assistance. Approach the load, crouch, grip firmly, align the back and lift gradually while straightening the legs; reverse to lower. Avoid full hot-liquid pots and allow for movement/splashing. Even eight-tenths full may be heavy/unstable: change quantity or method rather than lifting unchanged.

rst31-cooking1-cart-dry-kitchen.title: Check trolley exceptions and dry floors
rst31-cooking1-cart-dry-kitchen.text: Normally push a trolley while looking ahead; pulling reduces control and can hide obstacles behind you. The source gives cautious pulling on downward slopes or steps as an exception, not a safe method for every trolley/slope. First confirm a safe procedure for the route, model and load and whether assistance is needed. Overhigh loads can fall with small vibrations and obstruct vision. A dry kitchen keeps floors dry; wet floors risk falls and food contamination from bacterial/mould growth areas. Warn passers-by about spreading water, remove it under store procedures and restore dryness.

rst31-cooking1-blade-attendance-manual.title: Check blade-machine attendance and instructions
rst31-cooking1-blade-attendance-manual.text: Trained personnel use rotating-blade machines with specified checks such as pointing and calling. Do not leave the station while running or put hands into moving interiors. When leaving, follow the model’s required shutdown/isolation, such as switching off and unplugging. For washing, switch off, unplug and wait for complete blade stop. Use any safety devices as specified before removing/washing blades by the trained method. Read available instructions before use. Similar appearance does not establish the same disassembly method: compare the new manual and training with the responsible person.

rst31-cooking1-dish-wash-dilution.title: Check dish materials and chemical-preparation charts
rst31-cooking1-dish-wash-dilution.text: High dish stacks are unstable. Ceramic and glass differ in strength and can crack or break on impact, so the source describes washing separately by material. Do not use chipped/cracked items; after nearby breakage check for attached fragments and also withhold items that cannot be checked adequately. Detergents/disinfectants have product-specific concentrations; display clear dilution instructions so everyone prepares them consistently. Measure against labels/charts to avoid overly strong solutions harming hands or weak ones failing treatment. Remove moisture from alcohol-treated surfaces as directed and do not spray near flames.

rst31-cooking1-fire-prevention-detail.title: Separate flame, cigarette and electrical checks
rst31-cooking1-fire-prevention-detail.text: Smoke only in designated non-kitchen places and keep them orderly. The source’s closing example puts cigarette ends/matches in a dedicated lidded water-containing can, confirms extinguishment and disposes daily; actual disposal follows store/fire-service directions. Stay with frying and keep combustibles away from ranges. Keep flammable sprays away from sunlight, flames and other heat; manage waste oil in lidded containers away from ignition. Do not handle electrical equipment with wet hands; pull the plug body, not the cable. Shutdown after work, discontinuing frayed cords and preventing plug/socket dust are fire precautions too. Check flames and electrics separately at closing without leaving unverified areas.

rst31-cooking1-extinguisher-basics.title: Extinguisher basics and evacuation priority
rst31-cooking1-extinguisher-basics.text: Know extinguisher locations/labels and practise their use. The basic sequence shared by the source and Fire and Disaster Management Agency is remove the pin, aim the hose nozzle at the fire’s base, then squeeze the lever. Aim at burning material, not flame tips. Equipment labels, suitable fire types, an escape route and surrounding safety are prerequisites; this does not replace practical training. If fire is strong or reaches the ceiling, do not persist: alert people and evacuate. Do not cross smoke/flames to retrieve an extinguisher; follow store reporting/evacuation procedures.

rst31-cooking1-index-uguisu-context.title: Separate an index-only bone term from the body text
rst31-cooking1-index-uguisu-context.text: The source index contains “uguisu bone,” while the general fish-part diagram labels “cheek bone” without explaining equivalence. A separate Shimonoseki City source uses “uguisu bone” for a head-side bone in prepared migaki pufferfish. Do not substitute cheek bone from a similar term; ask which fish and processing state the instruction concerns. This clarifies terminology context, not pufferfish-processing qualifications, safety or knife-based bone-removal procedures.

rst31-cooking1-q001.stem: Which beef description and dish example match the source?
options: Chuck roll has no fat and is only for frying
Sirloin is fine-textured with steak examples
Tenderloin is tough/sinewy and only for soup
Rib loin is coarse and only for stir-fries
reasons: Chuck roll has moderate fat/flavour and shabu-shabu examples.
Sirloin is fine-textured with steak/roast-beef examples.
Tenderloin is tender and lean, not soup-only.
Rib loin is fine-textured with steak examples.
rst31-cooking1-q001.explanation: Check texture, fat and use together; cut descriptions do not establish safe heating criteria.

rst31-cooking1-q002.stem: You check an order against the pork table. Which explanation fits?
options: Outside leg has fatty layers and dongpo-pork examples
Leg is the most sinewy and only for long braises
Loin is leanest and always used identically to tenderloin
Shoulder has cubed-stew examples and loin has tonkatsu examples
reasons: Outside leg is mild lean meat; dongpo pork is a belly example.
Leg is lean and fine-textured, not only for long braising.
Loin has moderate fat, unlike tenderloin’s fat profile.
Shoulder matches stew and loin matches tonkatsu examples.
rst31-cooking1-q002.explanation: Check animal, cut and dish together.

rst31-cooking1-q003.stem: For steamed egg custard, which chicken cut is the source’s leanest example?
rst31-cooking1-q003.objective: Distinguish chicken texture and dish uses.
options: Wing
Thigh
Tenderloin
Breast
reasons: Wings are a collagen-rich example.
Thigh has richness from fat within the meat.
Tenderloin is the leanest example and is listed for steamed custard.
Breast is lean too, but tenderloin is the source’s leanest.
rst31-cooking1-q003.explanation: Chicken cuts differ; select the one suited to the dish.

rst31-cooking1-q004.stem: Which set is listed as summer seafood examples?
options: Japanese amberjack, oysters and snow crab
Sawara, wakame and asari clams
Ayu, Japanese flying squid, scallops, Japanese sardine and Japanese jack mackerel
Bonito, Pacific saury and chub mackerel
reasons: These are winter examples.
These are spring examples.
This matches the five summer examples.
These are autumn examples.
rst31-cooking1-q004.explanation: The table is a season guide; actual seasons also vary by origin and climate.

rst31-cooking1-q005.stem: Which spring/autumn pairing matches the source?
options: All species are identical in both seasons
Spring:salmon only; autumn:red sea bream only
Spring:Pacific saury/chub mackerel; autumn:wakame/funa carp
Spring:wakame/funa carp/red sea bream; autumn:salmon/Pacific saury/chub mackerel
reasons: The source gives different representatives by season.
Salmon is an autumn example and red sea bream a spring example.
The seasons are reversed.
Both match their seasonal columns.
rst31-cooking1-q005.explanation: Check species names; seasonal categories do not guarantee raw-food safety or freshness.

rst31-cooking1-q006.stem: When copying the winter column to a preparation sheet, which set contains only source examples?
options: Ayu, Japanese flying squid and scallops
Bonito, Pacific saury and chub mackerel
Sawara, funa carp and wakame
Pufferfish, cod species, hatahata, hokke, tuna species and kuruma prawns
reasons: Summer examples.
Autumn examples.
Spring examples.
All are winter examples.
rst31-cooking1-q006.explanation: This tests seasonal-table reading, not pufferfish qualifications or safe processing procedures.

rst31-cooking1-q007.stem: Which set is classified as root vegetables in the source?
options: Potato, taro, turnip and burdock
Strawberry, melon and watermelon
Green pepper, chilli and pumpkin
Mizuna, fuki and crown daisy
reasons: These match the source’s root-vegetable examples.
These are fruit-like vegetables in the source.
These are fruiting vegetables in the source.
These are leaf/stem vegetables in the source.
rst31-cooking1-q007.explanation: Read the source’s classification without independently replacing it with botanical generalisations.

rst31-cooking1-q008.stem: Which group is listed as leaf/stem vegetables?
options: Cabbage, onion, lettuce, fuki, crown daisy and mizuna
Lotus root, burdock and turnip
Melon, watermelon and strawberry
Edamame, broad beans and green beans
reasons: The source’s leaf/stem examples.
Root-vegetable examples.
Fruit-like vegetable examples.
Fruiting-vegetable examples.
rst31-cooking1-q008.explanation: Colour or appearance alone is insufficient; compare the source group and name.

rst31-cooking1-q009.stem: Which set fits the fruiting-vegetable column?
rst31-cooking1-q009.objective: Read bean/pod examples within fruiting vegetables.
options: Melon, strawberry and watermelon
Green pepper, chilli, pumpkin, green beans, edamame and broad beans
Burdock, turnip and lotus root
Fuki, negi and mizuna
reasons: Fruit-like vegetable examples.
All are source fruiting-vegetable examples.
Root-vegetable examples.
Leaf/stem vegetable examples.
rst31-cooking1-q009.explanation: The source includes these beans in fruiting vegetables; do not mix classification systems.

rst31-cooking1-q010.stem: Which seasonal pairing matches the vegetable/fruit table?
rst31-cooking1-q010.objective: Read spring/summer vegetable and fruit examples.
options: Spring:chestnut/persimmon; summer:daikon/Chinese cabbage
Spring:bitter melon/peach; summer:broad bean/strawberry
Spring:broad bean/strawberry; summer:bitter melon/green pepper/peach/cucumber/tomato/watermelon
Both seasons always contain only identical foods
reasons: Autumn/winter examples are mixed in.
The source seasons are reversed.
Both columns match.
The source separates representative seasonal examples.
rst31-cooking1-q010.explanation: This season guide does not deny year-round distribution or regional differences.

rst31-cooking1-q011.stem: Which explanation matches the vegetable/fruit columns?
options: Autumn:sweet potato/chestnut/persimmon/pear/shimeji/ginkgo; winter includes broccoli/negi
Autumn kaki always means oyster
Autumn:broccoli/negi; winter:chestnut/pear
Broccoli/negi are autumn-only examples
reasons: This matches both seasons.
In this vegetable/fruit column it means persimmon.
The first are winter and the second autumn examples, reversed here.
The source lists broccoli/negi for winter.
rst31-cooking1-q011.explanation: Read the classification column; identical readings need not mean the same food.

rst31-cooking1-q012.stem: In a kitchen without enough separate benches, work changes from ingredient preparation to plating. Which action fits?
options: Change the bench colour instead of washing
End raw preparation, wash surfaces/tools and disinfect as needed before switching
Have the same person do both simultaneously on one bench
Only wipe visible dirt with a cloth
reasons: Colour changes do not guarantee cleanliness.
This meets shared-equipment task-change conditions.
This conflicts with separating place/time to prevent secondary contamination.
This does not justify omitting washing/necessary disinfection.
rst31-cooking1-q012.explanation: Prevent ingredient contamination reaching food immediately before eating.

rst31-cooking1-q013.stem: After checking cut dimensions, which reading is appropriate?
rst31-cooking1-q013.objective: Distinguish source dimensions from store directions.
options: Give tanzaku and hyoshigi identical cross-sections if lengths match
Read 1 cm dice and roughly 3 cm shikishi squares as examples and check the store recipe
Make every cut a 1 cm square
Skip store samples once source numbers are found
reasons: This confuses flat tanzaku and stick-shaped hyoshigi.
This distinguishes examples from actual specifications.
This ignores different shapes/dimensions.
Store recipes and samples still need checking.
rst31-cooking1-q013.explanation: Source dimensions are not compulsory specifications for every recipe.

rst31-cooking1-q014.stem: You studied the rice example of at least 98℃ for 20 minutes and boiling-water additives. Which understanding is correct?
rst31-cooking1-q014.objective: Do not replace safety criteria with quality examples.
options: Vinegar brightens only green and baking soda only white
These are safe centre-heating limits for every food
Add equal quantities of salt/vinegar/baking soda to every ingredient
It is a rice-starch example; distinguish each additive’s purpose
reasons: This reverses the source’s white/green effects.
Do not generalise rice quality into all-food safety criteria.
Conditions/amounts depend on ingredients and recipes.
This preserves the rice context and separate additive functions.
rst31-cooking1-q014.explanation: Check cooking-quality explanations separately from hygiene criteria.

rst31-cooking1-q015.stem: What does the source’s roughly 180℃ frying-oil value indicate?
rst31-cooking1-q015.objective: Separate oil temperature from centre temperature.
options: An oil-temperature example
A post-cooking refrigerator setting
A centre-temperature pass value for every food
A setting required for every dish
reasons: About 180℃ is an oil-heating example.
It is not a refrigerator temperature.
Oil and food-centre temperatures differ.
It is not universal across dishes/equipment.
rst31-cooking1-q015.explanation: Do not record an oil example as a centre-heating pass/fail value.

rst31-cooking1-q016.stem: How should the example of long cooking around 70–80℃ be understood?
rst31-cooking1-q016.objective: Understand the scope of simmering-quality descriptions.
options: No centre check is needed
Every meat is always safe at this temperature
Treat it as a texture example and check hygienic heating separately
Every simmering liquid always has this temperature
reasons: A quality example does not replace centre-heating checks.
The source does not guarantee every meat’s safety.
This distinguishes quality and hygiene contexts.
The source separates normal boiling from lower-temperature examples.
rst31-cooking1-q016.explanation: Understand aims such as limiting tissue tightening and follow validated store processes.

options: Gas range:gas; IH/Chinese gas range:electricity
Gas/Chinese gas ranges:electricity; IH:gas
Gas/IH ranges:gas; Chinese gas range:electricity
Gas/Chinese gas ranges:gas; IH:electricity
reasons: The Chinese gas range source is wrong.
These sources reverse the classifications.
IH is electric and Chinese gas ranges use gas.
This matches the source classifications.
rst31-cooking1-q017.explanation: Similar bench-shaped equipment still requires heat-source/process checks on labels/manuals.

rst31-cooking1-q018.stem: Which description fits equipment organised by use?
rst31-cooking1-q018.objective: Separate washing/hand units from food-processing machines.
options: A small processor cuts small ingredients; an automatic hand unit treats hands
An automatic hand unit washes dishes
A small washer cuts small vegetables
A door-type washer dispenses hand disinfectant
reasons: Targets and uses both match.
Hand equipment is not for food processing.
It automatically washes small tableware.
It washes dishes and utensils.
rst31-cooking1-q018.explanation: Do not judge only by “automatic” or “small”; check what is treated.

rst31-cooking1-q019.stem: Familiar kitchen work becomes busy. Which response matches the safety approach?
rst31-cooking1-q019.objective: Judge haste, familiarity and clothing checks.
options: Tread down heels for easier, safer shoe removal
Experienced workers skip safety checks
Keep every step despite haste and wear specified clothing/shoes correctly
Replace the uniform freely with personal clothes
reasons: Treading heels down increases fall risk.
Familiarity does not justify omitting checks.
This checks both procedures and clothing.
Do not independently replace specified clothing.
rst31-cooking1-q019.explanation: Do not reduce safety actions because of haste, assumptions or familiarity.

rst31-cooking1-q020.stem: How should body-weight ratios, an eight-tenths-full pot and slope trolley examples be read?
rst31-cooking1-q020.objective: Do not universalise source figures or exceptions.
options: An eight-tenths-full pot never spills
Check health, load configuration, route and equipment procedures, not examples alone
Anyone can carry alone below the example figure
Every trolley is safe on slopes using one method
reasons: Movement and weight still change risk at eight-tenths.
This distinguishes examples from actual safety checks.
Body weight alone does not establish strain or stability.
Model, slope and load conditions cannot be ignored.
rst31-cooking1-q020.explanation: Do not turn examples into universal limits or operating procedures.

rst31-cooking1-q021.stem: A first-time slicer looks like the previous model. What is appropriate?
options: Put fingers into moving parts if it sounds quiet
Skip the manual if appearance is similar
Check the manual/trained method and apply specified shutdown/isolation even when leaving
Leave it rotating while doing other work
reasons: Never put hands into moving interiors.
Appearance alone does not establish the method.
This meets model-specific pre-use and leaving conditions.
This conflicts with remaining at the operating station.
rst31-cooking1-q021.explanation: Do not assume identical safe operation/isolation from similar appearance.

rst31-cooking1-q022.stem: Which name matches the ingredient in Figure A?
rst31-cooking1-q022.objective: Match ingredient appearance with source names/classification.
options: Oyster
Scallop
Asari clam
Snow crab
reasons: Oyster shells are rough and irregular.
The fan-shaped shell and white adductor example is a scallop.
Asari are small oval bivalves.
Snow crab is a long-legged crustacean.
rst31-cooking1-q022.explanation: Match representative appearance to the name and source classification/season examples. Check actual condition, variety differences and safety separately.

rst31-cooking1-q023.stem: Which pairing matches Figure B and the source classification?
rst31-cooking1-q023.objective: Match ingredient appearance with source names/classification.
options: Aubergine—fruiting vegetable
Carrot—leaf/stem vegetable
Cucumber—fruit-like vegetable
Onion—root vegetable
reasons: The purple fruit/green calyx is aubergine, classified as fruiting vegetable.
It is not carrot, which the source classifies as root vegetable.
It is not cucumber, which is classified as fruiting vegetable.
It is not onion, which is classified as leaf/stem vegetable.
rst31-cooking1-q023.explanation: Match representative appearance to the name and source classification/season examples. Check actual condition, variety differences and safety separately.

rst31-cooking1-q024.stem: Which Figure C ingredient and source season pairing matches?
rst31-cooking1-q024.objective: Match ingredient appearance with source names/classification.
options: Negi—summer
Fuki—winter
Bamboo shoot—autumn
Asparagus—spring
reasons: The clustered tip differs from negi leaves; negi is a winter example.
This is not a fuki leaf-stalk example.
It is not a thick-sheathed bamboo shoot, which is also a spring example.
The green clustered-tip stem is asparagus, a source spring example.
rst31-cooking1-q024.explanation: Match representative appearance to the name and source classification/season examples. Check actual condition, variety differences and safety separately.
